extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (patent prosecutors and litigators), USPTO practitioners, IP counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of AIA-era post-issuance proceedings (Post-Grant Review, Inter Partes Review, Supplemental Examination, Transitional Program for Covered Business Method patents) covering timing, grounds, burdens, amendment rights, and interplay with litigation and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review (PGR) scope and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Applies to patents issued from applications having an effective filing date of March 16, 2013 and later; conducted before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB); allows a third party to contest validity of an issued patent; limited window – 9M from issuance; any grounds of invalidity may be asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR is analogous to European opposition proceedings; because it allows any ground it is broader than IPR in scope. The 9-month filing window from grant is jurisdictional to PGR.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR petition threshold and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Petition must demonstrate likelihood that at least one of the challenged claims is unpatentable or raise 'a novel or unsettled legal question that is important to other patents or patent applications'; burden of proof on petitioner — 'preponderance of the evidence'; cannot appeal PTO’s decision regarding whether to grant PGR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution requires showing more than a bare challenge; the standard at institution differs from final proof, which is preponderance at the merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR — patent owner amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owner has two months to file preliminary response; allowed 1 motion to amend by cancellation of any challenged claim and, for each challenged claim, can propose substitute claims; subsequent motions may be entered upon joint request of the parties or for good cause; substitute claims cannot expand scope or introduce new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment opportunities are limited: initial motion is essentially the primary chance to amend; substitute claims must be commensurate with original disclosure. Entry of later motions is narrowly circumscribed.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR procedural flexibilities and bars
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO can consolidate multiple PGR proceedings; may be terminated upon joint request of petitioner and patent holder, unless PTO has already decided the merits; cannot institute PGR if petitioner has already filed a district court action challenging validity (declaratory judgment). If civil action alleging infringement filed within 3 months of patent grant, court cannot use PGR petition as basis to stay consideration of a preliminary injunction motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic interactions with district court litigation affect availability and timing of PGR; consolidation is an administrative tool PTO may use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review (IPR) applicability and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Replaces inter partes reexamination; effective September 16, 2012 and applies to all patents regardless of filing date; can only be filed after the PGR window has closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR is the successor to inter partes reexam for post-grant challenges based on printed publications and patents. Timing relative to PGR is important — IPR is available after PGR opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR institution standard (§314(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition' — this replaces the older 'substantial new question of patentability' standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a heightened institution standard compared to the old SNQ test; the PTO applies a 'reasonable likelihood' test at institution for IPRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR grounds limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent can be contested in IPR based on lack of novelty or non-obviousness evidenced by submitted patents or printed publications; limited to published patent documents and printed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike PGR (which allows any grounds), IPR is limited to prior-art publications and patents as the basis for invalidity challenges at institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and differing standards across proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Burden of proof rests on the petitioner; PGR merits decision uses preponderance of the evidence, while institution standards differ (e.g., 'reasonable likelihood' for IPR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish institution thresholds from the ultimate merits standard: institution may require a lower or different showing than the preponderance standard applied at final decision for PGR.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR rulemaking topics (Sec. 316/326)
rubrics_metrics.description: Director shall make rules to govern PGR proceedings including: making the file public except when intent to seal; establishing standards for sufficient grounds for instituting review; setting standards for discovery of relevant evidence; prescribing sanctions for abuse of discovery; providing for protective orders; establishing standards for patent owner to amend patent; providing either party with right to oral hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are procedural protections and constraints that the PTO will flesh out by rule; discovery and amendment standards are notable areas of substantive PTO regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR timeline and statutory time limits
rubrics_metrics.description: 9-month window to file PGR petition; patentee given period for preliminary response; decision whether to institute PGR within 3 months of preliminary response; conclusion within 1 year with possible 6-month extension for good cause; inter partes review can be filed only after expiration of period for PGR; PTO can limit number of inter partes reviews filed in first four years after enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory deadlines are tight: institution and final decision timing is compressed, with limited extension possibilities. Strategic timing (e.g., filing within 9 months) is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB responsibilities and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 7 replaces the BPAI with the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) whose responsibilities include reviewing adverse decisions of examiners on written appeal, reviewing appeals of reexaminations, conducting derivation proceedings, and conducting inter partes and post-grant reviews; parties can appeal decisions to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB consolidates appellate and trial-like functions at the PTO; its decisions are reviewable at the CAFC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental Examination — availability and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Only available to patent owner; allows owner to file a request for reexamination of an issued patent in order to cure any subsequently found defects; affirmative measure — not reactionary; cannot institute proceedings if patent owner has already been charged with withholding art; can initiate proceeding to inoculate patent against possible charges of inequitable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental examination is a defensive tool for patent owners to address prior art/information to reduce risk of unenforceability based on inequitable conduct (subject to exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental Examination — process and estoppel/effect
rubrics_metrics.description: If substantial new question of patentability is raised by additional art, Examiner may order reexamination of the patent; submitted information is not limited to published patent documents and printed publications; patent shall not be held unenforceable based on the information considered or corrected (exception — material fraud).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental exam can trigger reexamination and can shield the patent from unenforceability based on the considered information, but does not protect against fraud or material misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional Program for Covered Business Method Patents (CBM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 establishes a post-grant review proceeding for review of validity of covered business method patents; effective September 16, 2012 and applies to any business method patent regardless of issue date; limited window – 8 years; addresses invalidity based on prior art only, not subject matter eligibility; can only be used if petitioner has been sued for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBM proceedings are a time-limited transitional path to challenge business-method patents but exclude challenges based on subject-matter eligibility and are tied to actual litigation against the petitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/exclusions for Covered Business Method patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered business method patents do not include those for 'technological inventions'; 'Nothing in this section shall be construed as amending or interpreting categories of patent-eligible subject matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is statutory language shielding broader patent-eligibility doctrine from being altered by the CBM rules; technological inventions are excluded from CBM coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay with litigation — stays and estoppel (RORCHR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case automatically stayed if PGR filed (not just counterclaims) until patent owner moves to lift or files infringement action (or if petitioner moves to dismiss action); regarding infringement actions, a court cannot base a stay of preliminary injunction <3M post grant on the PGR. Estoppel applies in both PTO and courts as to petitioner — 'raised or reasonably could have raised' (RORCHR). For inter partes reexamination the old two-way estoppel lacked the 'reasonably' qualifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR/IPR create strong litigation effects: automatic stays and broad estoppel applying both before the PTO and in courts. The 'reasonably could have raised' wording expands estoppel scope compared to earlier regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of post-issuance proceedings (who/what/when/where/why)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarizes differences: Who — generally third party for PGR/IPR/old inter partes; Supplemental exam is patent owner; What — PGR: preponderance on any grounds; IPR: reasonable likelihood to prevail on publications; When — PGR: 9M post-grant; IPR after PGR period; Supplemental exam anytime (subject to sunset for some programs); Where — PTAB; Why — invalidate/intervening rights, inoculate or amend, business-method review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this comparative framework to choose the appropriate post-issuance option depending on timing, grounds, and the actor (third party v. patent owner).
